title.en: The odd numbers to thirty-three, the multiples of four to forty-eight, and twelve names

summary: The last anuvāka of the Chamakam asks for numbers: the odd numbers from one to thirty-three, then the multiples of four from four to forty-eight, each with ca me. Sāyaṇa says only that the words denote numbers; the Brāhmaṇa he quotes explains the two series as a pair, the odd numbers giving the metres dear to the gods and the even those dear to men, with thirty-three the number of the gods and forty-eight the syllables of the jagatī. It ends with twelve names, vāja to adhipati, without me, which Sāyaṇa reads either as food and what produces it or as the names of the twelve months. With the eleven anuvākas, he says, the vasordhārā is offered, one continuous oblation of ghee.

vyakarana.note: Feminine of eka. With tisraḥ (f. of tri) and catasraḥ (f. of catur, unit 3) it shows that the numbers are thought of as feminine; from five on the n-stem numerals do not mark gender.
n-stem pañcan; nominative plural pañca, without ending (so sapta, nava, ekādaśa …).
In the compound the first member eka has a long final, ekā-; tri takes the form trayas- (trayo- before d). Compound-internal sandhi stays as written.

translation.literal: One and for me, three and for me, five and for me, seven and for me, nine and for me, eleven and for me, thirteen and for me, fifteen and for me, seventeen and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May one be mine, and three, five, seven and nine, eleven, thirteen, fifteen and seventeen.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa says only that the words from ekā on denote numbers: «एकादिशब्दाः संख्यापराः». The rest of his comment reports the Brāhmaṇa on this anuvāka. The odd series and the even are offered ‘for pairing’ («मिथुनत्वाय»): the odd numbers, beginning ekā ca me tisraś ca me, are ayugma («विषमसंख्यारूपमयुग्मं»), the even yugma, and the two series, differing from each other like woman and man, make a pair: «राशिद्वयं स्त्रीपुरुषवत्परस्परविलक्षणत्वान्मिथुनत्वाय संपद्यते». By the odd numbers, he explains, the metres dear to the gods are produced: «विषमसंख्याया देवानां प्रियाणि च्छन्दासि निष्पाद्यन्ते».

flags.note: The compound numerals (ekādaśa, trayodaśa, ekaviṃśati …) are classed here as dvandva, the members being added; the grammatical tradition also analyses such numerals with an elided middle word (‘ten increased by one’). The meaning is the same either way.

vyakarana.note: ‘Nine and ten’, nineteen: the Vedic form, kept as it stands (later usage also has ūnaviṃśati).
viṃśati ‘twenty’ is a feminine noun in -i, nominative singular viṃśatiḥ; the compound numerals take its gender and number. So triṃśat, a feminine t-stem, nominative triṃśat.
tri becomes trayas- in the compound (trayo- before the voiced v of viṃśati, trayas- before t).
The last me stands after the pañcāśat mark [19]: no sandhi is made across it.

translation.literal: Nineteen and for me, twenty-one and for me, twenty-three and for me, twenty-five and for me, twenty-seven and for me, twenty-nine and for me, thirty-one and for me, thirty-three and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May nineteen be mine, and twenty-one, twenty-three, twenty-five, twenty-seven and twenty-nine, thirty-one and thirty-three.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa adds nothing on these numbers beyond his note that the words denote numbers («एकादिशब्दाः संख्यापराः»). The Brāhmaṇa he quotes gives the reason the odd series ends here: one offers up to thirty-three, because the deities are thirty-three, and so secures the deities. Each series rises, number after number, and the Brāhmaṇa says the two are made to increase in this way for going forward.

flags.note: corrections.json, C11.2: the second witness has एकत्रिँश्च्च, with a letter missing; the base witness's एकत्रिँशच्च (ekatriṃśat, ‘thirty-one’, in the series of odd numbers) is kept. Classed as a W2 error.

vyakarana.note: Feminine nominative plural of catur, like tisraḥ in unit 1.
Nominative of aṣṭan, ‘eight’, in its form aṣṭau (beside aṣṭa).
In the compound numerals dvi becomes dvā- and aṣṭan aṣṭā- (dvādaśa, aṣṭāviṃśati, dvātriṃśat).
ṣaṣ + daśa gives ṣoḍaśa, an irregular compound form (o for a, ḍ for ṣ-d).

translation.literal: Four and for me, eight and for me, twelve and for me, sixteen and for me, twenty and for me, twenty-four and for me, twenty-eight and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May four be mine, and eight, twelve and sixteen, twenty, twenty-four and twenty-eight.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa, reporting the Brāhmaṇa, calls this series, beginning catasraś ca me ’ṣṭau ca me, the even one: «समसंख्यारूपं युग्मम्». Its numbers rise from each to the next, four to eight and eight to twelve, and by the even numbers the metres dear to men are produced: «समसंख्यया तु मनुष्यप्रियाणि». By reciting both series the sacrificer obtains both («अतस्तदुभयं प्राप्नोति»).

sandhi.rule: final t before c becomes c (P. 8.4.40); so throughout this unit: -triṃśac ca, -catvāriṃśac ca

A feminine t-stem, ‘forty’; nominative singular catvāriṃśat.

translation.literal: Thirty-two and for me, thirty-six and for me, forty and for me, forty-four and for me, forty-eight and for me [may they be ready].
translation.readable: May thirty-two be mine, and thirty-six, forty, forty-four and forty-eight.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa quotes the Brāhmaṇa on why the even series stops at forty-eight: one offers up to forty-eight because the jagatī metre has forty-eight syllables and cattle belong to the jagatī («जगती जागताः पशवः»), so by the jagatī the sacrificer secures cattle.

vyakarana.note: suvar is the Yajurveda form of svar (MW: suvar, ind. = svar). In pause suvaḥ, so suvaś ca. Here it stands in a list of nominatives; Sāyaṇa takes it as the sun.
n-stem mūrdhan, nominative singular mūrdhā.
The text writes ñ after ś (श्ञ), the South Indian Taittirīya spelling of śn; the word is vyaśniya, and the padaccheda keeps the text's letter. Not in MW.
A patronymic in -āyana from āntya (MW), as bhauvana is from bhuvana: each derived name stands before the name it comes from.
Here there is no me: each item is followed by ca alone, and the last ca closes the Chamakam.

translation.literal: Food and impulse and the later-born and resolve and heaven and the head and Vyaśniya and Āntyāyana and Āntya and Bhauvana and Bhuvana and the overlord [may all be mine].
translation.readable: May food be mine, and impulse, the later-born, resolve and heaven, the head, Vyaśniya, Āntyāyana and Āntya, Bhauvana and Bhuvana, and the overlord.

units.traditional: Here me is absent, and Sāyaṇa supplies the sense: «वाजादयः सर्वे मम सन्त्विति शेषः» — ‘may all these, vāja and the rest, be mine’ is to be understood. He glosses only the first five: vāja is food («वाजोऽन्नम्»), prasava its production («प्रसवस्तस्योत्पत्तिः»), apija its production again and again («अपिजस्तस्यैव पुनः पुनरुत्पत्तिः»), kratu a resolve or a sacrifice (संकल्पः … यागो वा), and suvaḥ the sun, the cause of its production (हेतुरादित्यः). He then gives a second reading: the words are names of the months beginning with Caitra («अथवा वाजादयश्चैत्रादिमासानां नामविशेषाः»), and the sentence is completed ‘may they all be pleased’ («तदानीं ते सर्वे प्रीणन्त्विति वाक्यशेषः»). The ca's join the items to one another, or bring in deities of time and the like that are not named («चकाराः परस्परसमुच्चयार्था अनुक्तकालादिदेवतासमुच्चयार्था वा»). The Brāhmaṇa he quotes says that these twelve are offered because «द्वादश मासाः संवत्सरः», and by them the sacrificer stands firm in the year. Sāyaṇa's viniyoga closes the Chamakam: with the eleven anuvākas from the beginning the vasordhārā is offered as one continuous oblation of ghee: «अनुवाकैर्जुहोत्येकामाहुतिं संतता घृतात्».
units.reflection: The last list has no ‘for me’: twelve names stand side by side, joined only by ‘and’, and the asking falls silent.

flags.note: corrections.json, C11.5: the base witness writes व्यश्ञियश्च (ñ after ś, the South Indian Taittirīya spelling), the second witness श्न; the word is the same (vyaśniya). Classed as orthographic.
vyaśniya is not glossed by Sāyaṇa and has no entry in MW; Keith leaves it untranslated. The word table gives no meaning beyond ‘a name’.

The Saṃhitā's cāntyāyanaś cāntyaś does not show whether the two words begin with a or ā (ca + a and ca + ā both give cā). The padaccheda follows MW, which records Āntya and Āntyāyana for the TS; Sāyaṇa does not gloss them.

Sāyaṇa gives two readings: the twelve words as food, its production, its renewal, resolve and the sun (he glosses only these five), or as names of the twelve months. The translation renders the words by their dictionary senses and leaves the names (Vyaśniya … Bhuvana) untranslated.
